questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How parents can help teenagers plan and do their homework
How the teenage brain is still developing
questions.why: Neil says teenagers' brains are still developing in areas that control behaviour.

questions.q: How does Rob describe himself as a teenager?
questions.why: Rob says he was 'a nightmare', rude to his parents and never did his homework.

questions.q: According to Neil, why might teenagers' bad behaviour not be directly their fault?
options: They spend time with the wrong friends
questions.why: Neil says it's 'our brains' fault', because teenagers' brains are still developing.

questions.q: When were the first research papers on brain development in adolescence published?
questions.why: Professor Blakemore says the first papers were published in the late 90s.

questions.q: What did textbooks say when Professor Sarah-Jayne Blakemore was at university?
options: The brain keeps changing throughout life
Most brain development happens in the first few years
Teenagers' brains are the same as adults' brains
The brain develops most of all when people are in their twenties
questions.why: She says the textbooks claimed most brain development happens in the first few years.

questions.q: What is Professor Blakemore's opinion of that old belief?
questions.why: She says 'That dogma is completely false.'

questions.q: What does the prefrontal cortex help us to do?
questions.why: She says it is involved in high-level tasks 'such as decision making and planning'.

questions.q: What does Professor Blakemore suggest about expecting teenagers to plan their homework?
options: It is good training for their brains
It might be too much for them
Parents should do it for them
questions.why: She says it 'might be too much' because the planning part of the brain is not developed yet.
